summary: Specifies the Media Resource Control Protocol Version 2 (MRCPv2), which lets client hosts control media service resources such as speech synthesizers, recognizers, verifiers, and identifiers located in servers on the network. It is not a stand-alone protocol and relies on other protocols such as SIP. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: It is a remote control for talking machines. A program can tell a server to read text aloud or to listen and work out what someone said.

questions: how to control speech recognition servers
how does mrcpv2 use sip and sdp
subtitle: A text protocol for telling speech servers to talk, listen, record and recognize voices, set up over SIP.

tldr.problem: Phone and voice applications need speech synthesizers, recognizers, recorders and speaker verifiers, but those engines often sit on separate specialized servers that the application has to control over the network.
tldr.mechanism: MRCPv2 uses SIP and SDP to set up a control channel per resource, then sends text-based requests, responses and events over TCP or TLS, while audio travels separately over RTP.
tldr.outcome: It gives clients one common way to start speech output, collect recognition results, record audio and verify speakers. It is a Proposed Standard, and it does not interoperate with the earlier MRCP (version 1).

facts.label: Control transport
facts.value: TCP or TLS (servers MUST support TLS)

facts.label: Discard port in client SDP offer

today: RFC 6787 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2012. The metadata for this unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the specification of MRCPv2. It does not replace the earlier MRCP of RFC 4463, which it explicitly does not interoperate with.

sections.title: Why MRCPv2 Exists
sections.content:
MRCPv2 (Media Resource Control Protocol Version 2) lets a client device control media processing resources on the network: speech recognition engines, speech synthesis engines, and speaker verification and identification engines. The RFC says this makes it possible to build distributed Interactive Voice Response platforms, for example with VoiceXML browsers, while keeping the speech processing on specialized servers.

It is based on the earlier MRCP described in RFC 4463, but only as input. The method names look alike, yet the way they are carried is different, and there are more resources and more methods. The RFC states that there is no expectation that an MRCPv2 client will work with an MRCPv1 server or the reverse, and there is no migration plan or gateway definition.

The first version ran over RTSP (RFC 2326). MRCPv2 does not, because the consensus when the work began was that using RTSP this way would break it or cause backward-compatibility problems. Instead MRCPv2 builds on SIP (RFC 3261) and SDP (RFC 4566). It is not a stand-alone protocol: SIP and SDP set up the sessions, and MRCPv2 exchanges do not change the state of the SIP dialog or the media sessions.
sections.eli5: Some machines are good at speaking and listening, and your program may be somewhere else. MRCPv2 is the language your program uses to ask those machines to do their job.

sections.title: Architecture and Resource Types
sections.content:
A system has a client that needs to produce or consume media streams and a media resource server that has the engines to process them. The client uses SIP and SDP (with the offer/answer model of RFC 3264) to open an MRCPv2 control channel. Servers are addressed with ordinary SIP URIs such as sip:mrcpv2@example.net. Audio does not travel on the control channel: it goes between the server and a media source or sink, using RTP.

An MRCPv2 server may offer one or more of these resources:

  • Basic Synthesizer: builds speech only from concatenated audio clips and MUST support the SSML tags <speak>, <audio>, <say-as> and <mark>.
  • Speech Synthesizer: renders speech from text and MUST have full SSML support.
  • Recorder: records audio and gives back a URI to the recording.
  • DTMF Recognizer: extracts key-press tones from the media stream and matches them against a digit grammar.
  • Speech Recognizer: turns audio into recognition results, with semantic interpretation and optional enrolled grammars.
  • Speaker Verifier: checks a claimed identity by matching speech against stored voiceprints.

A client can discover what a server offers with a SIP OPTIONS request. The server answers with SDP that has a single m= line of media type application and one resource attribute for each resource it supports.
sections.eli5: Think of a call center with specialist helpers: one who reads aloud, one who listens, one who records, and one who recognizes voices. You ask the front desk which helpers are available.

sections.title: Setting Up Control Channels with SIP and SDP
sections.content:
MRCPv2 needs a connection-oriented transport such as TCP for reliable, ordered delivery of control messages. Clients and servers MUST implement TLS as well. Several channels can share one connection, and each message carries a channel identifier so the receiver can tell them apart.

Each resource gets its own control channel, set up by an SDP offer in a SIP INVITE or re-INVITE. The rules for the control m= line are specific:

  • There MUST be one m= line per resource, with media type application and transport TCP/MRCPv2 or TCP/TLS/MRCPv2.
  • In the client's offer the port is the discard port (port 9 for TCP). The server's answer carries the TCP port it listens on.
  • The client names the resource type in a resource attribute. The server answers with the full Channel-Identifier in a channel attribute, such as 32AECB234338@speechsynth.
  • The client's a=setup is active and the server's is passive, following RFC 4145. For TLS, RFC 4572 applies.
  • The first offer MUST use a=connection:new. Later offers may say new or existing to share a connection.

A client cannot allocate more than one resource of each type. To release a resource it sends a new offer with the control m= line port set to 0. To end everything it sends a SIP BYE. If either side notices that the connection for a channel was closed without a re-INVITE closing it, it MUST send a BYE for the whole dialog.

A cmid attribute ties a control channel to the mid of an audio m= line, so one audio stream can serve several resources or each resource can have its own. If the server can neither multiplex nor mix several resources onto one stream, it MUST reject the offer with SIP 488.
sections.eli5: Before talking to a helper, you first ring a front desk (SIP). The desk gives you a secret room number and a phone line for just that helper. Voices travel on a separate line.

sections.title: Messages: Requests, Responses and Events
sections.content:
MRCPv2 has three kinds of message: requests from client to server, responses from server to client, and asynchronous events from server to client. Each is a start-line, header fields, an empty line and an optional body. Text is UTF-8 and lines end in CRLF. The complete ABNF in Section 15 is the normative definition.

The start-line has the version (MRCP/2.0), a message-length that MUST be the second token, and then:

  • a request: method name and request-id;
  • a response: request-id, a 3-digit status code and a request state;
  • an event: event name, request-id and request state.

The request-id is an unsigned 32-bit integer chosen by the client. Clients MUST use monotonically increasing request-ids within a session, and a server that sees a duplicate or out-of-order one MUST reject it with 410. Responses and events carry the request-id of the request they belong to.

The request state is PENDING (queued and processed first-in-first-out), IN-PROGRESS (being processed) or COMPLETE (finished, so no more events for that request-id). Every message MUST carry the Channel-Identifier header field.

Many definitions are borrowed from HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2616) rather than copied. Header fields follow the format of RFC 5322, and their names are case-insensitive.
sections.eli5: Every message is like a letter with a first line saying who it is for and what it asks, a list of details, and then the main text. The server answers with the same request number so you know which question it is replying to.

sections.title: Generic Methods, Headers and Results
sections.content:
Two methods work on every resource. SET-PARAMS sets session parameters such as voice characteristics or recognition timers. The server returns 200 if it set everything, or 201 if it ignored some optional header fields that could safely be ignored. GET-PARAMS reads the current values: the server fills in each header field the client sent empty, or all settable parameters if none were named. The RFC says the wildcard form can be expensive and RECOMMENDS that clients not use it often. Values set with SET-PARAMS do not override ones given on an individual request.

For bad header fields the server answers 404 (illegal value), 403 (unsupported header field) or 409 (unsupported value), and echoes the offending fields. Other generic header fields include Active-Request-Id-List (which queued or running requests a request affects, or which ones were affected), Proxy-Sync-Id (used to coordinate barge-in between servers), Content-Type, Content-ID, Fetch-Timeout, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie and vendor-specific parameters.

Recognition, enrollment and verification results are carried as XML. The default is NLSML (Natural Language Semantics Markup Language), media type application/nlsml+xml, which all recognizer and verifier servers MUST support. Its root element is <result>, with <interpretation>, <enrollment-result> or <verification-result> children. EMMA can be used instead if negotiated in SDP with a=resultformat:application/emma+xml.
sections.eli5: Some commands work on every helper, like asking it to change its settings or to tell you its settings. Results come back in a tidy, labeled form that programs can read.

sections.title: The Speech Synthesizer Resource
sections.content:
The synthesizer takes marked-up text from the client and produces a stream of synthesized speech in real time. The main request is SPEAK, whose body is typically SSML (application/ssml+xml). Other methods are STOP, PAUSE, RESUME, BARGE-IN-OCCURRED, CONTROL and DEFINE-LEXICON. It sends two events: SPEECH-MARKER and SPEAK-COMPLETE.

If the resource is idle, SPEAK gets a success response with state IN-PROGRESS. If it is already speaking or paused, the response is PENDING and the request waits in a strict FIFO queue. If the current SPEAK fails, all queued ones are cancelled and each produces a SPEAK-COMPLETE with cause cancelled. When voice settings conflict, the order of precedence is: speech markup first, then header fields on the SPEAK request, then session defaults from SET-PARAMS.

STOP without an Active-Request-Id-List terminates all outstanding SPEAK requests, and the response lists the ones that were stopped. PAUSE or RESUME with no active SPEAK gets 402. Barge-in happens when the caller starts talking over a prompt: if a SPEAK has kill-on-barge-in enabled and BARGE-IN-OCCURRED arrives, the synthesizer MUST stop streaming audio at once and terminate any queued speech. The client MUST still send BARGE-IN-OCCURRED after a recognizer's START-OF-INPUT even if the two resources interact directly.
sections.eli5: You give the speaking machine a script and it reads it out. If you give it several scripts it reads them one after another. You can tell it to stop, pause or carry on, and it stops right away if the caller interrupts.

sections.title: The Speech Recognizer Resource
sections.content:
The recognizer receives an incoming voice stream and gives the client an interpretation of what was said. It covers two resource types: speechrecog (speech and DTMF) and dtmfrecog (DTMF only, ignoring speech). Its methods are DEFINE-GRAMMAR, RECOGNIZE, INTERPRET, GET-RESULT, START-INPUT-TIMERS and STOP, plus five optional methods for voice-enrolled grammars. It sends START-OF-INPUT, RECOGNITION-COMPLETE and INTERPRETATION-COMPLETE events.

In normal mode all speech or DTMF is matched against the grammar, and a no-match is returned if it fails or times out. In hotword mode the recognizer only looks for specific words or sequences and ignores the rest. The RFC also describes voice enrollment (building personal grammars from a caller's voice) and interpretation of plain text with INTERPRET.

RECOGNIZE carries the grammars in its body, either inline, as a text/uri-list, or as a text/grammar-ref-list that allows weights. Earlier grammars take precedence over later ones. Large grammars can be sent ahead with DEFINE-GRAMMAR and referenced later through the session URI scheme. On success the server answers IN-PROGRESS; if it cannot start it answers 407 with a Completion-Cause.

Timers decide how recognition ends. The No-Input-Timer ends it with no-input-timeout. The Recognition-Timeout starts when speech or a digit is detected. Once enough speech has matched, the Speech-Complete-Timer ends with success, or the Speech-Incomplete-Timer ends with partial-match. The final RECOGNITION-COMPLETE event carries a Completion-Cause such as 000 success or 001 no-match, and the NLSML result.
sections.eli5: The listening machine is given a list of things it should expect to hear. It listens to the caller, picks the best match, and tells you what it thinks was said and how sure it is. If nobody speaks for too long, it says so.

sections.title: The Recorder Resource
sections.content:
The recorder captures received audio (and optionally video) and stores it as content that a URI points to. The RFC names two main uses: capturing speech that may be submitted for recognition later, and recording voice or video mail.

A recorder MUST provide endpointing, meaning it can suppress silence at the start and end of a recording, and it MAY suppress silence in the middle. If it does, it MUST keep timing metadata that shows the actual timestamps of the recorded media. Its methods are RECORD, STOP and START-INPUT-TIMERS, and its events are START-OF-INPUT and RECORD-COMPLETE. Completion causes include success-silence, success-maxtime, no-input-timeout, uri-failure and error.
sections.eli5: The recorder is a tape recorder that skips the quiet parts at the start and end, and then gives you the address where the recording is kept.

sections.title: Speaker Verification and Identification
sections.content:
Speaker verification compares a recorded utterance with a stored voiceprint tied to a claimed identity. It usually has a designation phase, to establish the claimed identity, and an execution phase, in which a voiceprint is either created (training) or used to authenticate. Speaker identification associates an unknown speaker with a member of a population without a claim of identity. One set of methods handles single verification, multi-verification, group authentication and identification, by taking a list of voiceprint identifiers and returning scores.

The verifier's methods are START-SESSION, END-SESSION, QUERY-VOICEPRINT, DELETE-VOICEPRINT, VERIFY, VERIFY-FROM-BUFFER, VERIFY-ROLLBACK, STOP, CLEAR-BUFFER, START-INPUT-TIMERS and GET-INTERMEDIATE-RESULT. Its events are VERIFICATION-COMPLETE and START-OF-INPUT. A verifier can share a session with a recognizer only if both are allocated from the same SIP dialog.

The verifier owns a verification buffer where speech from a recognition or recording can be stored for later verification or training. Only one operation can touch the buffer at a time; another one fails with status 402.
sections.eli5: Your voice is a bit like a fingerprint. The verifier keeps a sample of how you sound and checks whether a new voice matches it, or which of several saved voices it matches best.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC treats MRCPv2 data as sensitive: recognition output, verification results, text sent for synthesis, personal grammars, spoken audio, recordings and voiceprints. It points readers to the security discussion in RFC 4313.

  • Session setup: SIP implementations MUST support SIP digest authentication and sips URIs, and SHOULD use them. When TLS is used the client MUST verify the server's identity.
  • Control channel: clients and servers MUST support TLS and SHOULD use it by default unless other protection such as IPsec is used.
  • Media: servers and clients that handle audio MUST support a mechanism to protect it, such as SRTP (RFC 3711).
  • Content by URI: implementations MUST implement HTTPS for indirect content access. Servers must be ready for clients that point them at slow or problematic documents, and should be cautious about large Fetch-Timeout values.
  • Stored media: recordings and voiceprints can present substantial privacy and impersonation risks if stolen.

The RFC also notes that it does not mandate how DELETE-VOICEPRINT requests are authorized; in practice each voice biometric provider uses its own mechanism.
sections.eli5: Voices and recordings are private. So the conversations should be locked, the other side should prove who it is, and saved recordings should be kept safe.
